sm: Joe Rogan and guest Mike Baker open with small talk about Baker's mustache, which began as a growing contest with his nineteen year old son, and about Halloween costumes, with Baker dressing as Wyatt Earp. They joke about westerns and how unpleasant the past really was, with disease and body odor. Rogan describes landing in New York just before airlines were grounded. They then discuss the recent run of outages at airlines, Microsoft, banks and Apple. Baker says the frequency illusion makes people see a pattern, and that infrastructure is old and cobbled together, though it is right to ask whether attacks were involved.

Baker continues on the outages, saying maintenance rushes before the release of a big video game may have played a part, and that hackers and state actors were watching how fragile and non-redundant systems are. They move to AI, including concerns about models escaping sandboxes and the talk of an AI bubble, with companies valued far above their revenue, as in the dot com era. Rogan then turns to the midterm losses, blaming the Iran war and tough hemp and THC laws, which he links to the alcohol lobby. They discuss weight loss drugs cutting alcohol use, and Baker describes cutting carbs after a pre-diabetes warning from his cardiologist.

Baker says he lost twelve pounds in about four and a half weeks by cutting bread, pasta, rice and desserts, while still allowed a martini. Rogan argues marijuana laws should match federal rules, noting how illegality forced cannabis businesses into cash, and Baker compares that to carrying sacks of payroll cash in Iraq. Rogan worries about young people embracing socialism and about New York disbanding its terrorism response unit in favor of unarmed public safety officers. They look up a news story about two private security officers being shot at a housing complex, and Baker admits he had only glimpsed the coverage on a television.

Rogan says socialism has never worked because those in charge become corrupt, and both men call for term limits and for mental fitness standards for politicians. They discuss the lobbying revolving door, and Baker says his company's first investors were lobbyists, good people in a flawed industry. They talk about Mitch McConnell's health and his wife Elaine Chao, and about an Idaho senator reelected at age eighty three. The conversation drifts to Chinese and Russian spies who blend into American society, and the FX show The Americans, with Baker noting the FBI handles most counterintelligence on American soil.

Rogan and Baker discuss a doubtful proof of life photo and criticize aides telling aging senators how to vote. They talk about politicians' sudden wealth, and Ilhan Omar's reported finances and the allegations about her immigration history. Baker predicts little consequence from Washington, saying investigations there go to die. The talk turns to Jeffrey Epstein, including a new article questioning the autopsy. They point out camera failures, missing guards, a former cellmate who was a convicted killer, and a pathologist who said the neck fractures looked more like strangulation than hanging. Baker says Epstein's death is like UFOs, impossible to dismiss without enough evidence.

The two keep discussing details of Epstein's death, including the autopsy, the cell, and the pathologist who has struggled to publish findings. Rogan brings up Mark Middleton, a former Clinton aide linked to Epstein, found dead in Arkansas in 2022 with an extension cord around his neck and a shotgun wound, with the gun thirty feet away. Rogan argues a shotgun could not fly that far, and says the investigators were either crooks or scared. Baker says he had not looked deeply into the Epstein case, but that reading more shows why it cannot be dismissed as conspiracy talk.

They look into a link between the cellmate accused of trying to kill Epstein, Nicholas Tartaglione, and Ghislaine Maxwell through a shared attorney, and note that prosecutors dropped the death penalty against Tartaglione in December 2022. He was convicted in 2023. Rogan then criticizes Governor Newsom for commuting the sentences of everyone on California's death row. They debate whether prisons should rehabilitate or punish, and agree that people who kill should stay locked up. Rogan praises rehabilitated former inmates, but says prisons are not set up for that, and raises the problem of private prisons.

Rogan says private prisons made jailing people profitable, and prison guard lobbies favor marijuana laws that keep prisons full. He and Baker describe the difficulty of reversing entrenched corruption, citing stories from Tulsi Gabbard. Baker then turns to Nvidia and Jensen Huang, saying the White House shifted from toughness on China to supporting chip sales during 2025, around the time of a twenty five million dollar donation to the ballroom. He alleges that Chinese intelligence used Alice Wang, an executive, to get close to Huang, and says Nvidia's systems for spotting diversion of its chips were faulty.

Rogan explains Nvidia's history from gaming graphics cards to AI, and shows a chip he received from Huang. He relays Palmer Luckey's view that China actually blocks imports of Nvidia chips, with six hundred thousand H200 chips stuck at a port, because Beijing wants its own domestic industry. Baker agrees but says this ignores years of Chinese espionage. They discuss Huang's sixteen hour days and sixty direct reports, and a story about Chinese students at Berkeley panicking during an internet outage because they could not check in with handlers, which the transcript's own search says was never confirmed.

They discuss a report of the United States allowing six hundred thousand Chinese students, and the Chinese influence funding in academia. Baker explains why Alice Wang's role in setting up a firm with Alibaba as its anchor customer would be valuable to Chinese intelligence, since Alibaba has alleged ties to the Chinese military. They recount how Jack Ma criticized Beijing, saw his big public offering halted, and was fined about 2.8 billion dollars before reappearing quieter. Baker says Chinese spies would not need Huang to hand over files, only to talk about meetings, dinners and chip policy, and he says promotions would have followed in Beijing.

Rogan and Baker debate whether Huang had a relationship with a spy and an employee, how overwork can warp judgment, and whether Nvidia can replace a founder who has run it for thirty three years. Baker says an intelligence service does not need to recruit an unwitting contact, and that Wang looked more like an access agent than a trained officer. Baker adds that no one is indispensable, and that the company may benefit from depending less on one person. Rogan compares it to SpaceX and Elon Musk, and notes the tech community rallied around Huang once the story broke.

They continue on whether Nvidia's board acted rightly, noting that the New York Times reported a video it had not seen and that neither person had confirmed the affair. They compare Huang to Dana White and Steve Jobs as hard to replace. Baker then describes China's influence efforts at state and local levels, such as the case of the Arcadia, California mayor accused of spying, and grassroots groups targeting phosphate mining in Florida. They recall Eric Swalwell's reported relationship with Fang Fang, and joke about how attractive alleged spies are.

They look up Fang Fang and joke about spies' looks, then check on Elaine Chao, who was born in Taipei, Taiwan, and has no known Chinese spy link. They recall Anna Chapman and the Russian sleeper agents arrested in 2010, who were sent home in a prisoner swap. Baker explains how an access agent works, first meeting a person of interest, then handing that person to a better placed officer who gradually assesses, tasks and perhaps recruits them. He says not every Chinese student is a spy, but some are, and Chinese students need party approval to study abroad.

Rogan says few American students go to China, so honeypot operations would be one sided, and brings up a Chinese American physicist, Ning Li, who worked on anti-gravity research in Alabama. Rumors say she vanished to China after a breakthrough, but her son said she turned down a Chinese offer and she died in America at seventy eight. They discuss the physicist who first raised the rumor, and recent UAP file releases from the Pentagon, which Baker calls uninteresting. Baker agrees that the government likely holds secret technology, from his own experience with the agency's science group.

Baker floats a scenario in which American intelligence asked a scientist to return to China to learn what the Chinese were doing, though he says he is only speculating. Rogan raises the 2024 New Jersey drone sightings, with his friends describing huge silent craft, and Baker says the government could have cleared it up by briefing Congress, and that it may have involved counter-drone testing. They then discuss Iran, with strikes on Riyadh's tallest building, Bahrain and Kuwait, and Baker says there has been months of tit for tat fighting despite the White House saying the war is over.

Baker says the White House was drunk on its Venezuela success, with the capture of Maduro, and underestimated Iran, which has killed thousands of its own protesters. He predicts an unsatisfying deal in which Iran stops disrupting the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for an end to the American blockade, some unfrozen assets and eased sanctions. He says three carrier groups there are costly, shipping and insurance remain jittery, and Iran is running a disinformation campaign about tankers. He thinks Tehran will wait out negotiations until the Democrats take Congress in January, and that the White House will give concessions that will be hard to present as victory.

They discuss whether regime change in Iran would lead anywhere good, comparing it with Venezuela, where the same security figures remain and American interest centers on oil and drugs. They talk about American strikes on suspected drug boats, which continue though they get less coverage. Rogan then raises a drop in violent crime since Trump took office, and Baker credits more police on the streets. An AI search tool cites FBI estimates that violent crime fell 9.3 percent in 2025, the largest annual drop since 1936, and Rogan says the media ignores it.

Baker credits cooperation among local, state and federal police for the drop in crime, and both men hope Democrats stay moderate after the midterms, with Baker doubting the Democratic Socialists will have much sway. They discuss young people's malaise, noting that the average first time home buyer is about forty, and that people feel advancement is out of reach. They disagree with the advice to just skip coffee and avocado toast, though Baker says saving matters. They also touch on the stock market and on Trump owning Nvidia shares.

Baker says young people are dropping out, choosing van life, and having fewer children, with immigration crackdowns also lowering birth rates. They worry about the celebration of political violence on the left, citing Luigi Mangione and the Charlie Kirk killing, and discuss why people resent health insurers, Obamacare, and claim denials. Rogan tells of a fence company owner whose insurer threatened to drop him over a twenty thousand dollar claim. Baker describes being rear ended on September 11 in his wife's Porsche Taycan, which was totaled, and a long wait while insurers dragged out a settlement.

Baker finishes the car story, saying the at-fault driver's insurer paid, his wife bought another Taycan, and they have become converts to electric cars. They discuss AI tools used by insurers to deny claims, with Rogan citing a Stanford report on weak oversight of AI in prior authorization. They talk about Luigi Mangione, and the dangers of political violence from any side. They also debate voter ID, proof of citizenship, and voter fraud, with Baker saying the truth lies between the left and hard right, and Rogan says California made it illegal to show ID to vote, and now requires ID to buy creatine.

They talk about California's age limit on creatine, which Rogan says is a safe and beneficial supplement, and call the state a nanny state. They move to kratom, with Rogan noting that Chris Bell recently described his own addiction, and that gas stations in Idaho sell it. Baker says he relies on his wife to handle healthcare and the household, and describes how complicated it is to navigate care alone. He is curious how voters will react to Democrats' Medicare for all, citing long waits in Britain's national health system, and calls for public and private cooperation with better regulation.

Baker argues against removing private insurance, saying government does little well and that profit motive drives people like Jensen Huang, and he adds that he has never seen socialism work, including in Scandinavia. They then discuss reports that eleven National Security Agency and Cyber Command workers died by suicide over about a year, ten of them near Fort Meade, which has drawn congressional scrutiny. Baker says intelligence workers avoid admitting mental health struggles for fear of losing assignments, so such problems get glossed over, and the pattern needs a counterintelligence look.

Baker says the cluster of suicides must be examined for foreign involvement, though he is not claiming there was any. He compares it to Epstein, saying the government fuels conspiracy theories by withholding files, and that releasing Epstein and UAP files would help. They agree the Epstein files, along with the Iran war, inflation and the ballroom, contributed to the midterm loss, and they discuss weak candidates like Ken Paxton against Talarico in Texas. Baker says the pendulum of politics swings too far each way now, and they close with thanks and a joke about people assuming he is still a CIA handler.
